title.rendered: France, Nigeria partner to strengthen agric value chains

content.rendered:
France has strengthened its partnership with Nigeria to boost agricultural value chains by unveiling the France-Nigeria Agribusiness Club, a platform designed to connect the French-Nigerian business community, technical experts, the French Embassy and other stakeholders to drive investment, innovation and trade in the sector.

The announcement was made on Thursday during the inaugural France-Nigeria Agribusiness Series 1 held in Lagos, where French and Nigerian officials outlined plans to deepen co-operation in agribusiness through financing, knowledge transfer, technical support and market access.

Speaking at the event, the Consul General of France in Nigeria, Laurent Favier, said the partnership would combine Nigeria’s agricultural potential with French expertise to position the country as a major agri-food hub for Africa.

Favier said, “Nigeria has the potential of becoming one of the biggest agri-food hubs. Because you have this potential, we have the expertise, and together, we can make something brighter, stronger and deeper. Today, we are announcing something stronger in agribusiness because it is going to be a gateway for businesses in both our countries.”

He added that the newly launched France-Nigeria Agribusiness Club would provide a structured platform for businesses, the Franco-Nigerian Chamber of Commerce, the French Embassy, technical advisers, Business France and academic institutions to collaborate.

“Something was missing, which was a standing table where we can meet the chamber, experts, the embassy, the technical advisers and everybody around one table. Today, we have decided to organise and structure that through the France-Nigeria Agribusiness Club,” Favier said.

The diplomat noted that the club will also become part of the Franco-Nigerian Chamber of Commerce, with expectations of attracting more than 500 members.

Favier said France was also expanding financial support for African agriculture through the Food and Agriculture Resilience Mission Plus initiative and a €300m facility managed by Proparco to strengthen agricultural value chains across the continent.

He added that the initiative formed part of a broader €27bn commitment announced during the Africa Forward Summit in Nairobi to accelerate financing for African agricultural value chains and agri-food trade.

The Agriculture Counsellor for Nigeria, Ghana and Cameroon at the French Embassy in Abuja, Rachid Benlafquih, said France would help Nigerian farmers meet European Union export standards through training, technology transfer and stronger value chain development.

Benlafquih said, “France is the gateway to an even bigger EU market. We have many activities to bridge the French ecosystem with the Nigerian ecosystem to improve the huge potential of Nigerian agriculture through knowledge transfer, innovation transfer and better organisation of value chains.”

He disclosed that officials from Nigeria’s Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security and the Tomato Producers Association of Nigeria would travel to France to learn biocontrol technologies to tackle Tuta absoluta, a pest responsible for significant tomato losses.

Benlafquih also identified aflatoxin and Salmonella contamination in sesame and ginger as major obstacles to exports to Europe, saying France would work with Nigerian stakeholders to address the challenges.

He added that reducing post-harvest losses, strengthening cold-chain infrastructure, improving veterinary services and developing Nigeria’s fisheries and blue economy would significantly increase agriculture’s contribution to the country’s gross domestic product.

In her keynote address, the Dean of Lagos Business School, Pan-Atlantic University, Professor Olayinka David-West, said stronger partnerships and better data infrastructure were essential to unlocking investment in Nigerian agriculture.

She said, “The distance between the high-altitude promise and the ground-level reality of Nigerian agriculture is not primarily a distance of resources. It is a distance of information, institutions and partnerships.”

David-West noted that capital was available globally but investors were discouraged by fragmented and unreliable agricultural data, saying, “The binding constraint is not a shortage of capital. Global capital is abundant. The binding constraint is a shortage of investable propositions supported by evidence. Data infrastructure is investment infrastructure.”

She urged France and Nigeria to pursue joint research programmes, technical fellowships, certification initiatives and co-investments in processing and cold-chain infrastructure to build competitive agricultural value chains.

The Convener of the France-Nigeria Agribusiness Series and Chief Executive Officer of JR Farms, Olawale Rotimi, said the newly established club would co-ordinate existing partnerships and accelerate collaboration between stakeholders in both countries.

He said, “Everybody is now under one umbrella of the club. Our approach will be more coordinated, not scattered. We expect accelerated progress between France and Nigeria in the area of agribusiness.”
